# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book was written for the business engineering students at the University of Namur (UNamur),
but it stems from years of experience teaching introductory and advanced data analytics courses
across different institutions. There is no shortage of excellent books in this space: theoretical
handbooks like *An Introduction to Statistical Learning* build the statistical foundations
rigorously, and applied books like *Hands-On Machine Learning* cover the modeling toolkit in
depth. What none of them focus on is what business and economics students actually need most: the
tools and methods to turn a messy, real-world business problem into a proper data analytics
project. That is what this book tries to do differently. There is no lengthy mathematical
derivation here, but plenty of hands-on code, and the practical tips and tricks that make the
difference between a model that works on a slide and one that survives contact with a real
business problem.

## Who this book is for

This book offers a gentle introduction to Python, so no prior programming experience is required
to start. That said, a basic introductory programming or Python course would benefit the reader,
since the programming covered here is aimed squarely at what you need for data analytics, not the
general fundamentals of programming as such. A basic statistics course is similarly useful, since
not every statistical concept is re-derived from first principles. In practice, this makes the
book a good fit for undergraduate or Bachelor-level teaching once students have already had some
exposure to programming and statistics, even a light one.

## What this book covers

The book walks through a full data analytics pipeline, from raw, messy data to a working,
evaluated predictive model: Python fundamentals, data understanding, data exploration, data
preparation, model evaluation, and modeling. Each chapter pairs a concept with runnable code, so
the code is never a black box you're asked to accept on faith.

## How to read it

Chapters build on each other and are meant to be read in order. Each one comes with a companion
Jupyter notebook (`notebooks_student/`) so you can run the code yourself, not just read it. If you
want to run the code locally, the Installation Guide appendix walks through setting up everything
you need.
